summary: Sotorasib (Lumakras) is an oral covalent KRAS G12C inhibitor dosed at 960 mg once daily. As a single agent it treats KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC after prior systemic therapy, and with panitumumab it treats KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer after fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin-, and irinotecan-based chemotherapy. KRAS G12C status must be confirmed with an FDA-approved test. Key serious risks are hepatotoxicity requiring scheduled liver monitoring, interstitial lung disease/pneumonitis that can be fatal, and QTc prolongation. Acid-reducing agents and strong CYP3A4 inducers lower exposure and should be avoided or managed, and it can cause fetal harm.
indications: Treatment of adults with KRAS G12C-mutated locally advanced or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who have received at least one prior systemic therapy

Treatment of adults with KRAS G12C-mutated metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) who have received prior fluoropyrimidine-, oxaliplatin-, and irinotecan-based chemotherapy, in combination with panitumumab

If coadministration with a locally acting antacid cannot be avoided, give sotorasib 4 hours before or 10 hours after the antacid
Obtain liver tests before starting and monitor during treatment; evaluate new respiratory symptoms promptly for ILD/pneumonitis
moa: Sotorasib is a small-molecule covalent inhibitor of KRAS G12C. It binds irreversibly to the cysteine residue of the KRAS G12C mutant protein, locking KRAS in its inactive GDP-bound state. This blocks downstream oncogenic signaling through the RAF/MEK/ERK and PI3K/AKT pathways, inhibiting tumor cell proliferation and survival in KRAS G12C-mutant cancers while largely sparing wild-type KRAS. In colorectal cancer it is combined with the anti-EGFR antibody panitumumab to counter adaptive EGFR-mediated resistance.

absolute: Known serious hypersensitivity to sotorasib or any excipient
relative: History of QT prolongation, electrolyte disorders, or QT-prolonging drugs
Moderate to severe hepatic impairment (limited data; monitor closely)
monitor: Liver tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase) before and during treatment
ECG and electrolytes for QTc prolongation risk
Pregnancy status before starting; CBC and GI tolerance

preg: Based on animal findings and mechanism, sotorasib can cause fetal harm including embryo lethality. Verify pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential and advise effective contraception during treatment and for 1 week after the last dose.
lact: There are no data on sotorasib in human milk or its effects on the infant or milk production. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, advise women not to breastfeed during treatment and for 1 week after the final dose.
renal: No labeled dose adjustment for renal impairment. Not studied in severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease; use with caution and monitor closely.
hepatic: No labeled adjustment for mild impairment; not studied in moderate to severe impairment. Hepatotoxicity is a key risk - obtain liver tests before starting, monitor during treatment, and withhold, reduce, or discontinue for transaminase or bilirubin elevation per labeling.

major: Strong CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort) - decrease sotorasib exposure; avoid
Acid-reducing agents (PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids) - decrease sotorasib absorption; avoid or separate antacids (4 hours before or 10 hours after)
moderate: CYP3A4 substrates, especially narrow therapeutic index drugs (sotorasib induces CYP3A4 and may lower their exposure; adjust as needed)
P-gp substrates such as digoxin or dabigatran (sotorasib may increase their exposure; monitor)
QT-prolonging drugs (additive QTc risk; monitor ECG and electrolytes)
minor: Strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors such as itraconazole - no clinically significant effect on sotorasib; no dose change
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; high-fat meals modestly increase exposure without a labeled dose change
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; limit alcohol given hepatotoxicity risk and GI effects
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor liver tests, ECG (QTc) with electrolytes, and chest imaging or pulse oximetry if pulmonary symptoms arise

serious: Hepatotoxicity including grade 3-4 transaminase and bilirubin elevation
Interstitial lung disease / pneumonitis, including fatal cases
Severe diarrhea with dehydration and electrolyte loss
emergency: Yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe abdominal pain (liver injury) - seek urgent care
New or worsening cough, dyspnea, or fever (pneumonitis) - seek urgent evaluation
Fainting, palpitations, or irregular heartbeat (QT prolongation/arrhythmia)

monitoring: Liver tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin) before starting, every 3 weeks for the first 3 months, then monthly or as clinically indicated
Pulmonary symptoms; withhold and evaluate for ILD/pneumonitis and permanently discontinue if confirmed
ECG and electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) for QTc prolongation
GI tolerance, hydration, and electrolytes with diarrhea or vomiting
Pregnancy status before starting in females of reproductive potential
counsel: Take once a day at about the same time, with or without food; swallow tablets whole and tell your team if you cannot swallow them
Report yellowing of skin or eyes, dark urine, right-sided abdominal pain, unusual tiredness, or easy bleeding (possible liver injury)
Report any new or worsening cough, shortness of breath, or fever right away (possible lung inflammation)
Tell your team about fainting, palpitations, or an irregular heartbeat, and about all other medicines including antacids and herbal products
Use effective contraception and do not breastfeed; report severe diarrhea, nausea, or vomiting so it can be managed early
pk: Target inhibition within hours; tumor responses develop over weeks of daily dosing
Median plasma Tmax about 1 to 2 hours after oral dosing
Mean terminal elimination half-life about 5 hours
Once-daily dosing maintains target coverage despite the short half-life due to irreversible binding; steady state within about 3 weeks
Store at 20-25 C (excursions 15-30 C permitted) in original container; protect from moisture
pearls: First KRAS G12C covalent inhibitor; locks mutant KRAS in the inactive GDP-bound state - confirm KRAS G12C with an FDA-approved test before starting
Standard dose 960 mg once daily both as a single agent (NSCLC) and with panitumumab (mCRC); step down to 480 mg then 240 mg for toxicity

Hepatotoxicity can be severe - check liver tests before starting, every 3 weeks for 3 months, then monthly; withhold or reduce for transaminase elevation and add corticosteroids for significant events
ILD/pneumonitis can be fatal - withhold for any new respiratory symptoms and permanently discontinue if confirmed; risk higher after prior checkpoint inhibitor therapy
Acid-reducing agents lower exposure - avoid PPIs/H2 blockers and separate antacids (4 hours before or 10 hours after); strong CYP3A4 inducers lower exposure (avoid)
Embryo-fetal toxicity - verify pregnancy status and use effective contraception
missed: If you miss a dose and more than 6 hours remain before the next dose, take it as soon as you remember. If 6 hours or less remain, skip the missed dose and take the next dose at the regular time. Do not take two doses at once; if you vomit after a dose, do not repeat it - take the next dose on schedule.
overdose: There is no specific antidote for sotorasib overdose. Expected effects reflect exaggerated toxicities such as hepatotoxicity, GI effects, and pneumonitis. Provide supportive care with liver, pulmonary, cardiac (ECG), and electrolyte monitoring. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
